prompt.context: You have been hired by the head of business development at Electro-Growth, a large electronics manufacturer in the U.S. The company is interested in increasing its revenue by manufacturing new products. Currently, your division develops three kinds of products: (1) Innovative Products – Brand new products that represent 10% of all products your division produces; each Innovative Product developed is expected to generate $40M in new revenue. (2) New Versions of Products – New versions of existing products that represent 40% of all products your division produces; each New Version product is expected to generate $10M in new revenue. (3) Current Products – Current products represent 50% of all products your division produces and do not generate new revenue; they only guarantee consistent revenue from these products. You are contemplating restructuring your division to improve your capacity to produce new products. Currently, it takes your division 24 months to develop an Innovative Product and 12 months to develop a New Version of a product. After the restructuring it will take 18 months to develop both products.
prompt.question: Should Electro-Growth go ahead with the restructuring?

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs of restructuring?
clarifying_info.a: There is no cost for restructuring and no change in the cost structure after restructuring.

clarifying_info.q: Will the relative mix of products change after restructuring?
clarifying_info.a: No. There is no change in the relative quantities of each type of product — Innovative still represent 10%, New Version still represent 40%, Current still represent 50%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal of the restructuring?
clarifying_info.a: The only goal is to increase revenue from the development of new products.

framework: Potential Gains From Restructuring: more revenue from increased manufacturing of innovative products; improvement in company brand from having more innovative products

Potential Restructuring Costs / Difficulties: HR, R&D, and manufacturing costs of restructuring (note: interviewer confirms there are no costs); loss of revenue from existing products due to deprioritization; competitive response from other electronics manufacturers
Quantify net revenue impact: calculate yearly new-product revenue before vs. after restructuring to determine whether restructuring is worthwhile

questions.prompt: Calculate the total yearly new-product revenue BEFORE restructuring.
questions.guidance: Simplify by assuming the division produces 10 total products per cycle: 1 innovative (10%), 4 new-version (40%), 5 current (50%). Before restructuring: innovative takes 24 months so 0.5 innovative products per year; new-version takes 12 months so 1 new-version product per year per slot, giving 4 per year for the 4 slots. Yearly revenue = 1*(0.5)*$40M + 4*(1)*$10M = $20M + $40M = $60M.

math.setup: Assume 10 total product slots. Innovative: 1 slot, 24-month cycle = 0.5 products/year. New Version: 4 slots, 12-month cycle = 1 product/year each = 4 products/year.
steps: New Version yearly revenue: 4 slots * 1 product/yr * $10M = $40M

questions.prompt: Calculate the total yearly new-product revenue AFTER restructuring.
questions.guidance: After restructuring both product types take 18 months, so output rate = 2/3 products per year per slot. Innovative: 1 slot * (2/3) * $40M ≈ $27M. New Version: 4 slots * (2/3) * $10M ≈ $27M. Total ≈ $54M. Revenue actually falls.

math.setup: Both product types now take 18 months = 2/3 products/year per slot.
steps: New Version yearly revenue: 4 slots * (2/3) products/yr * $10M ≈ $26.7M

questions.prompt: Compare pre- and post-restructuring revenue and state a recommendation.
questions.guidance: Restructuring reduces annual new-product revenue from $60M to ~$54M — a decline of ~$6M/year. The candidate should clearly recommend against restructuring and explain why: slowing New Version development hurts more than speeding up Innovative Product development helps, because New Versions collectively contribute more revenue ($40M vs $20M) before restructuring.

math.answer: Revenue drops by ~$6M per year; do NOT restructure

brainstorming.prompt: If Electro-Growth still wants to grow revenue, what alternatives should it consider?

categories.name: Product Mix Shifts
ideas: Increase the share of Innovative Products beyond 10%
Reduce the share of Current Products to free capacity for revenue-generating lines

categories.name: Development Efficiency
ideas: Invest in R&D tools or processes to shorten development cycles independently of restructuring
Adopt agile/iterative development to get faster time-to-market

categories.name: Revenue per Product
ideas: Expand into adjacent markets to increase addressable revenue per product

categories.name: Partnerships & M&A
ideas: Acquire or partner with smaller innovators to bring more innovative products without internal cycle-time constraints
License technology to reduce development burden

recommendation: Electro-Growth should NOT move forward with the restructuring as planned
Restructuring reduces annual new-product revenue from $60M to ~$54M — a net loss of ~$6M per year
risks: Cancelling restructuring could cause stagnation in growth
Competitors may be pushing forward more innovative products, eroding Electro-Growth's market position
next_steps: Devise a new plan for increasing revenue that does not sacrifice New Version output
Look into increasing the proportion of Innovative Products developed, as they generate substantially more revenue per product
Continue researching ways to decrease development time for both product types without equalizing them at a slower rate
